note: Swappable grammar pack (R46, §9.3/§9.11) for the backup/archival line — the eleventh card, founded on its own verbatim §1.3 dominant verb, Schedule, the second ADR-0014 #D1 blessing and the first card of a verb that stood zero-claimed. Machine-checked wall between namespaces: 'decision' strings appear while the player decides or loses (labels, terms, refusals, alerts, status rungs) and stay SOBER per §9.3 clauses 2-3; 'flavour' carries the recognition comedy for quiet surfaces. Authenticity law for this line (§9.3/§9.11): the drama is PROOF AND TIME — the checkmark that means nothing, the band that closes at 06:00, the copy that is the one the attacker also has — and the ransomware beats are depicted only as consequence: a dwell day, a chosen restore point, a bill. No attack walkthroughs, no tool names, no cryptanalysis; the level teaches that 'verification is the only proof' (§1.3), not how to defeat it.

nodeId.desc: Board object the decision surface is about (vault aisle / robot rail / library row id).

availableAtTick.desc: Tick at which the queued intent or a freed hand presents.

slotName.desc: Socket designation on a node (drive bay, robot slot, tape library position).

jobId.desc: One scheduled backup job by designation — the visitor this line actually serves.

customerName.desc: A protected customer by name — the convoy's owner, the caller at 4am, the one whose worst day is your entire product.

windowHours.desc: Hours in the nightly band — the unit this line runs on ('Backup runs in hours (the window)', §7.8).

closeHour.desc: The hour the window band closes — 'Jobs that don't finish by 06:00 didn't happen' (§1.9 verbatim).

successNights.desc: Consecutive green checkmarks on a job's ledger — claims until proven, the card's own counter.

writeKb.desc: Kilobytes actually written on the success night — the 4KB classic, measured.

drillCostUsd.desc: Dollars a restore drill costs — money spent, revenue produced zero, the cost centre that is the only proof.

rtoHours.desc: Hours of Recovery Time Objective on the live clock — the hourglass the customer's business is measured against.

gbProtected.desc: Gigabytes under protection on the plan — half of the unit this line sells (§0.3: 'A GB + an RTO').

gbPerHour.desc: Measured restore rate, GB per hour — 'the number that matters', the computed half of an honest RTO (§Backup entry pass).

dedupPct.desc: Deduplication ratio as a percent — 'dedup ratio literally is your gross margin' (§1.3 verbatim).

retentionDays.desc: Days of retention the plan sells — the ladder pricing is played on.

dwellDay.desc: Day number inside the retention band an encryption timestamp reads back to — the dwell, counted in keep-days.

custodyChoice.desc: The key-custody stance chosen per plan tier: hold, don't-hold, or hand-over — the trilemma the doc makes a product decision.

surgeCustomers.desc: Customers restoring at once on the regional bad day — 'your restore capacity was sized for two'.

ticketId.desc: Customer support ticket number — the desk log of the line's real visitors.

hour.desc: Clock hour a convoy event or call lands at — the hour the band is open or shut.

day.desc: Day of the quarter, for the intern's log and the rewrite date on the tag.

hostName.desc: A vault or competitor in press/obituary copy.

decision.type.backup-archival.name: Restore Point
decision.type.backup-archival.codex: The Vault's floor: GB protected and restore SLA, sold on a promise — 'The product is not storage, it's restore time' (§1.3). Visitors are backup jobs: nightly convoys that must finish inside the window or fail and retry, invisibly until restore time. The core inversion: your success metric is something you can't observe — durability is a hidden stat revealed only by restore testing, which costs money and produces no revenue. Dominant verb: Schedule; the window is the constraint. Scoring is RPO/RTO, not uptime; the catastrophe never breaks availability — the readout is static.
decision.goal.backup-archival.binding: Night and proof, not cores and uptime: the band that closes at {closeHour} decides what you may promise, the durability that decides everything is hidden until you pay to see it, and the hands that walk the aisle at dusk are the same hands that answer the phone at four — the product is a Tuesday's file and the only instrument is yesterday's drill.
decision.scarce.backup-archival.qos: Nothing here is sheddable the way other lines shed, and the card counts that as the design: jobs are scheduled convoys, all-or-nothing chains, and an interrupted run is 'a partial failure that compounds into tomorrow's' (§3.2) — the BAND decides who didn't finish; the queue outside the closing edge is the whole QoS. The meter sells proof, not priority, and the shed order rides the standard P3-P0 law until the window-packing pass owns this line's ordering (§7.8).
decision.skin.backup-archival.inspector: Vault blue-white under label yellow: cold steel, deep blue, blue-white task lighting, a lot of empty floor — 'the slowest, calmest-looking level type, and that's the point, because the threat is invisible' (§1.3). Enormous inertia: the tape robot arm takes real seconds to travel and you watch it; restores are the only fast, warm thing here. The meters are the RTO hourglass, bit-rot tiles speckling grey, and the hand-written paper tag on the vault door, date crossed out and rewritten. The catastrophe never flashes red: the readout is static.
decision.economy.backup-archival.bad-month: A restore that fails in public (§6.6 Companion C, verbatim): one declared disaster, one hourglass, one console showing static where a customer expected Tuesday — and the quiet six-month arithmetic of every drill you skipped arriving in the forty seconds it takes to find out whether the last year of green checkmarks meant anything.
decision.cac.backup-archival.protection-cycle: §6.6 Companion B prices this family row directly: 'Backup / DR | $400–1,500 | 6–12 months | 0.1–0.3, spiking on restore' (:23378) — a four-figure desk sale, a protection conversation that takes most of a year to close, and a payback ratio the doc itself footnotes 'spiking on restore': the acquisition cost walks in the same door as the surge. The funnel is the worst-day pitch: sell the promise, price the proof, and know the egress bill is what keeps the account (§1.3 CEO truth).
decision.verbs.backup-archival.transfer.1: Window-thinking transfers everywhere: any line that fits work into a finite box now asks you the same question the band asks at dusk — what finishes tonight, what is deliberately left outside with a red seal, and what do you tell the person who discovers the schedule moved without telling them? The maintenance window was always a backup window with the paperwork filed under someone else's name (§1.9 Rosetta, different ink).
decision.relations.backup-archival.mastery: The vault reads the calendar the other way: drills booked before the doubt, retention priced before the dwell, checkmarks made solid with measured throughput instead of promises typed into a contract, and the tag rewritten so often that the worst day arrives to a room already walking the path — a durability bonus everywhere the operator earns in quarters that looked, to everyone else, like nothing was happening (§5.6 'Mastering Backup grants a durability bonus everywhere').
decision.relations.backup-archival.distillate: Playbook: buy proof before you need it — a restore drill is a recurring cost with zero visible benefit until the one day it is everything; treat every green checkmark as a claim until measured, every window as a promise someone will audit, and every retention day as a number the other side can read too; verification is the only proof, the window is the constraint, and nobody ever cared how fast you were — only whether Tuesday's file came back.
decision.handover.backup-archival.runs-out: The night. You never run out of disk — you run out of night; jobs that don't finish by {closeHour} didn't happen, and the band will not widen for anybody's feelings (§1.9's own backup handover, verbatim in shape).
decision.handover.backup-archival.kills-you: An unrestorable backup (§0.3 failure column verbatim): not an outage, not a storm — a readout showing static where a year of green checkmarks promised a file, discovered at restore time, in public, on the only metric that was ever being graded.
decision.handover.backup-archival.customer-wants: Tuesday's file: nobody cares how fast you are, they care whether it comes back — one crate, one chain, one red seal, one hourglass; the whole product is the answer to a phone call you hope never arrives (§1.9's own customerWants line, verbatim in shape).
decision.rosetta.backup-archival.window: The backup window is your maintenance window with the calendar weaponized (§1.9 Rosetta law, different ink): shared-web freezes the business day to touch the live floor; this line IS the frozen window — a Gantt-like bar every job on every board eventually learns it cannot overrun, because here the maintenance window does not protect the work from the customers, it protects the customers from the work.
decision.rosetta.backup-archival.gravity: The gravity lock is the renewal cliff with its polarity reversed: shared-web's cohort leaves at the cliff because renewal is cheap, and this line's cohort stays because leaving is the bill — 'the switching cost is the egress bill' (CEO truth §1.3) — so the date that renews the account is the date the customer last priced their own data going home.
decision.scenarios.backup-archival.restore-drill: The Restore Drill (§1.3 signature scenario verbatim frame): a customer declares a disaster at 4am, you have an RTO clock, and you must actually walk the restore path — find the cartridge, load it, read it, ship the data — while any shortcut taken in the last ten levels bites you now. The climax is always a real restore under a clock and the live question is whether the last year of green checkmarks meant anything. Consequence, not instruction: the path is walked, never diagrammed.
decision.scenarios.backup-archival.window-moved: The Backup Window That Moved (§2.9 verbatim title): daylight saving shifts the schedule, the nightly job now starts inside the business day, runs, 'succeeds', and saturates the array for four hours while customers work — no failure, no alert, the dots connected two days later by somebody with the invoices open. The scariest event on this line is a success in the wrong twelve hours.
decision.scenarios.backup-archival.hollow-checkma: The Hollow Checkmark (§2.9 'Backup That Never Restored' + §1.3 classic, verbatim cores): the job has been 'successful' for fourteen months writing a 4KB file, the checkmark drawn slightly hollow on inspection, and the game should let this happen — because the teaching is the fill-vs-stroke distinction itself, and the verify upgrade is the one that turns the hollow solid. The discovery belongs to the restore, always.
decision.alert.window-overrun: {jobId} on {nodeId}: the band closed at {closeHour} with the crate half-open on the belt — jobs that don't finish by {closeHour} didn't happen (§1.9 verbatim). The chain now carries a red seal into tomorrow, and tomorrow already has a convoy.
decision.alert.hollow-check: {jobId} reported success on {nodeId} for the {successNights}th night; measured write: {writeKb} KB. Green checkmarks are claims, not proofs — the only honest reading of this row costs {drillCostUsd} and is scheduled under the drill desk.
decision.alert.dwell-detected: Retention advisory for {customerName}: the encryption timestamp reads to day {dwellDay} of the sold {retentionDays} — the bad copy is inside the keep. The restore decision is now which of two dates to believe; both of them bill.
decision.alert.rto-clock: Restore request for {customerName}: RTO clock at {rtoHours} h against {gbProtected} GB protected. The hourglass does not negotiate; the measured {gbPerHour} GB/hour does the talking, and the only words it knows are done or not.
decision.alert.verify-invoice: Restore drill completed on {nodeId}: {drillCostUsd} spent, revenue produced zero. The durability figure you cannot observe just got one interval more provable — the cost centre is the instrument.
decision.terms.dedup-ratio: Dedup ratio — {dedupPct}% stored-twice-means-once: 'dedup ratio literally is your gross margin' (§1.3 verbatim). The slider every CFO plays on the back of physics; every point is a promise about how much of your fleet is fiction.
decision.terms.retention-window: Retention ladder — {retentionDays} days of keep priced as a lever, not a shelf ('retention policy is a pricing lever', §1.3). The day-400-of-365 request is this term read by a person having the worst week of their career; the ladder is also the attacker's calendar — dwell is measured in your own units.
decision.terms.key-custody: Key custody — {custodyChoice}, chosen per plan tier, visibly, at the Pricing Engine (§2.x verbatim law): hold it and you can always restore them, with breach exposure and a legal surface attached; refuse it and you sometimes say the unsayable sentence; hand it over and they will lose it. There is no fourth option and the doc says so.
decision.refusal.hands-exhausted: Both hands are committed. The {verb} intent is queued and presents when a hand frees at tick {availableAtTick}.
decision.refusal.stamped-in-future: The {verb} intent is stamped for tick {availableAtTick}, ahead of the current minute. Nothing was spent.
decision.refusal.unknown-node: No board object named {nodeId} exists at the current tick. Nothing was changed.
decision.refusal.edge-exists: A {relationKind} cable already links {nodeId} to those endpoints. The existing edge was left as it is.
decision.refusal.slot-occupied: {slotName} on {nodeId} is occupied. One supplier per socket; disconnect before you reconnect.
decision.status.rung-5: We are aware of the fire.

flavour.ticket.subject.hollow: green checkmarks every night — how do I actually see the files
flavour.ticket.body.hollow: Ticket {ticketId}, filed day {day}. I'm not saying your job failed. I'm saying it has been succeeding beautifully for longer than our company has existed and when I ask for one PowerPoint from a Tuesday you have checkmarked nine times, your console says four kilobytes. Please don't tell me it's compressed. Tell me when the drill is. Tell me the drill is Tuesday. — and yes, I have read your egress page, no, we are not leaving, we are ARRIVING, nightly, until somebody opens a crate.
flavour.ticket.subject.day400: deleted a table — need it back from day 400
flavour.ticket.body.day400: Ticket {ticketId}. Yes, the retention says {retentionDays}. No, I did not read the retention. The table is small and it is load-bearing and the intern is already crying, which I am mentioning for context, not sympathy. You invoice by the ladder; I am asking you to extend the ladder one rung by whatever means a human being with a console and a prayer can manage. Charge me the surge line. I have watched your webinar; I know what 'spiking on restore' means and I am choosing it.
flavour.ticket.subject.wrongvolume: the backup is perfect — ask me how I know
flavour.ticket.body.wrongvolume: Ticket {ticketId}. We verified it ourselves, beautifully: full success, zero errors, the whole checkmark arc lit up like a stadium. The only detail, and I say this with the affection of a long-time customer, is that the volume we have been protecting for three years is the one we renamed after the migration, and the volume we are currently on fire about has never been backed up a day in its life. The drills have been perfect. The drills have been drilling nothing. Send the invoice to the intern.
flavour.press.headline.publicfail: {hostName} confirms restore failure was never an outage — customers discover the product is a promise during a live incident page; the company's status feed, ironically, remained green.
flavour.press.headline.stoppedsix: {hostName} subscribers learn six months of quiet meant silence, not safety — the checkmark's long vacation ends in a press conference about what a green light is actually for.
flavour.forum.thread.verified: Anyone else started printing the drill date on the invoice line? 'Verified {day} days ago' sells itself; 'succeeded nightly' used to. We attach the hourglass reading to every plan renewal now. The customers read the crossed-out dates. They always read the crossed-out dates. Bought the second robot arm this quarter. Sleeps better.
flavour.forum.thread.rategb: Reminder that backup throughput and restore throughput are different sports: we sized the link on the nightly push and discovered our advertised tier implies {gbPerHour} GB/hour coming the OTHER way, which is a network design constraint, not a backup setting. The doc said so. The doc is smug about having said so.
flavour.chatter.desk.0600: 06:{hour} on the belt: last crate dropped with a clunk four minutes before the edge. The band closes like a question. Nobody on the floor cheers because nobody is on the floor at this hour — the vault keeps its own hours and we just answer them.
flavour.chatter.vault.static: The robot arm moved like it always moves. Fetched like it always fetches. Loaded like it always loads. And the readout showed us what static looks like when it has been holding a checkmark for fourteen months. The aisle was very quiet and very well-lit and that is the worst part: nothing in here ever said it was unhappy.
flavour.codex.window: The window is the constraint (§1.9 teaches-line verbatim): {windowHours} hours of night between dusk and the closing edge, every job in the game reduced to one question — are you inside the band or are you a story about the band. The Gantt bar is the level's floor plan; the red seal is its door.
flavour.codex.hollow: Verification is the only proof (§1.9 teaches-line verbatim): the checkmark is drawn by the job, about the job, on the job's own ledger — which is why the honest version costs money, walks the aisle at dusk, and comes back with a date written on paper. Success that cannot be rehearsed is not success; it is weather.
flavour.loading.tip.rto: RTO is a computed value, not a promise the player types in — measured restore rate against bytes protected, the doc's own honesty law. The hourglass on this floor is loaded with arithmetic. Everything else on the screen is marketing, including last night's checkmark.
flavour.loading.tip.proof: A backup is a theory. A restore is a fact. Between the two sits a robot arm, a tape, a courier, a key policy, and one clock that only runs during someone's worst night. The level is not about the writing. The level has always been about the reading.
flavour.intern.entry.tag: Day {day}: was asked to update the paper tag on the vault door. The senior tech watched me cross out a date and write today's and said, 'don't enjoy the crossing-out part.' Then he asked when the last one was rewritten. Then he walked the aisle to check. The tag says proof; the walk says whether the tag is telling the truth. I have learned there are two kinds of paperwork in this building.
flavour.intern.entry.clunk: Day {day}, {hour} at night: watched my first real convoy from the catwalk — crates rolling in under the band like weather going somewhere. Every one landed with a clunk and the last one I saw closed the gap at the edge so tight the light cut it in half. The senior tech said the sound is the whole job. Then a phone started ringing on the desk and nobody on the catwalk moved, because of course nobody moved, because it was the wrong hour for that sound and the right hour for nothing else.
flavour.sticky.note.tag: Taped to the inside of the vault door, hand-written: 'Jobs that don't finish by 06:00 didn't happen.' Below it, in the same hand: 'And the ones that did happen — PROVE one.' Nobody has taken them down since. — console note, post-drill
flavour.abuse.canon.dwell: Retention advisory for {customerName}: encryption timestamp reads to day {dwellDay} of the sold {retentionDays}. The request is legitimate, the restore point is contested, and the tone of this notice is deliberately the one your invoice also uses: we are going to read both dates back to you, in order, and bill whichever ladder you choose. This message is the proof rung, and the ladder thanks you for reading it in order.
flavour.abuse.canon.surge: Surge advisory: {surgeCustomers} customers are requesting restores at once — 'your product's busiest day is the day it is hardest to deliver' (§2.x verbatim). Fair-use egress terms apply and were chosen by you, at sign-up, in the same font as this sentence. The hourglass queue is first-in-first-out; the priority tiers are the ones you sold years ago, and — per the doc that wrote this crisis — you forgot about.
flavour.vendor.reply.firmware: Have you tried updating to the latest firmware?
flavour.vendor.reply.log-bundle: Please collect a full log bundle.
flavour.vendor.reply.known-issue: This is a known issue, fixed in the next release (no ETA).
flavour.canary.vault-tally: {successNights} green, {writeKb} KB, the band wide and the desk quiet on {nodeId} — the checkmark, the claim and the proof are the same instrument, read at three prices.
